A DbContext is not thread-safe, and a singleton is shared by every concurrent request. AddDbContext registers it as scoped, so each request gets its own instance.

Middleware runs in the order it is added. Authorization checks the user before authentication has read the cookie or token, so the user is still anonymous. The order is UseRouting, UseAuthentication, UseAuthorization.

explanation.en: Once the endpoint writes the body, the headers have been sent. OnStarting registers a callback that runs just before the headers go out, so it can still add X-Elapsed. Append and finally both run too late; flushing only sends the response sooner.

explanation.en: The request body is a forward-only network stream: once read, it is consumed. EnableBuffering makes it seekable (buffered in memory or on disk), so the middleware can rewind it for the endpoint. Synchronous reads are disallowed by Kestrel by default.

MVC cannot await an async void action, so it finishes the request at the first await, and the uploaded file may be disposed mid-save. Returning Task<IActionResult> lets the framework wait and turn exceptions into a 500.

answer: Make the lambda `async` and `await` the call

explanation.en: ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so .Result rarely deadlocks, but every waiting request blocks a thread-pool thread: thread-pool starvation. All three distractors still block. Awaiting frees the thread while the call is in flight.

options: Wrap the loop body in `try { ... } catch { }`

Loop on `stoppingToken` and pass it to `Task.Delay`
answer: Loop on `stoppingToken` and pass it to `Task.Delay`

explanation.en: On shutdown the host cancels stoppingToken and waits for ExecuteAsync to finish. This loop never looks at the token, so the host waits until its shutdown timeout. Checking it and passing it to Task.Delay ends the loop at once.
